newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair promises to "make a difference".
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair promises to "make a difference".

text.p: Britain's new Prime Minister Tony Blair on Wednesday unveiled an "ambitious but practical" legislative programme, including plans for major constitutional reforms, and promised clear leadership after his landslide election victory.

Britain's youngest prime minister this century told a packed House of Commons he would run a "people's government, rebuilding trust between government and governed" after Labour ended 18 years of Conservative rule on May 1.

The legislative programme, formally announced by head of state Queen Elizabeth in a glittering, ages-old ceremony in the upper House of Lords, set out 26 bills the Labour government hopes to enact over the next 18 months.

The package tackled Labour's five main election manifesto pledges -- to cut primary school class sizes, shorten hospital waiting lists, mete out swifter justice for persistent juvenile offenders, get 250,000 young people off welfare into work and create conditions for "lasting prosperity".

But there was also a number of eye-catching constitutional reforms to decentralise power, make government more transparent and clean up politics after a string of sex and money scandals during the Conservatives' last years in power.

Referendums will be held to approve plans for a tax-raising parliament in Scotland and a less powerful assembly in Wales. But the government did not put forward a bill to remove the voting powers of hereditary peers in the upper house, one of its aims while in government.
"The British people do not have false expectations," Blair told the opening session of parliament after the queen's speech.
"We will not put right the damage of 18 years in 18 days or even 18 months. But in 12 days we have already shown how we can make a difference. We have started...as we mean to go on."

In a whirlwind start to government, Blair's minister have instituted a number of significant changes, including allowing the Bank of England to decide interest rate changes, and have signalled a less confrontational foreign policy, particularly towards the European Union.
Saying the defeated Conservative government had lost touch with the "instincts and aspirations of the British people", Blair said the new government would reunite the country.
"Our mandate is clear: to modernise what is outdated, to make fair what is unjust; and to do both by the best means available, irrespective of dogma or doctrine, without fear or favour."
But Blair came under fire from former prime minister John Major, who claimed credit for leaving the Labour government with the best economic inheritance of any British government.

Major also accused Labour, which has moved to the centre ground of politics, of stealing many of the defeated government's policies and of failing to explain how it would pay for its health and education reforms.
"The road to hell is paved with good intentions and the...speech is full of good intentions," said Major.

Major, who has already announced he is standing aside as party leader, had never sat on the opposition benches since he became a member of parliament in 1979 in the election which began the Conservatives' stranglehold on power.
Blair, whose radical overhaul of the party was crucial to its victory, was surrounded by the massed ranks of Labour MPs who spilled over from the government benches.

With a majority of 179 in the 659-seat house, Blair is unlikely to have much problem pushing through his programme. Major acknowledged the scale of Blair's victory but appealed to his successor not to steamroller opposition parties.

The Liberal Democrats, who have 46 seats in the 659 seat House of Commons, also promised "cooperative and constructive opposition" if Blair kept to his promises to introduce a more open and inclusive style of government.
